summary: An April 1st joke RFC claiming that quantum entanglement will give some internet paths a round-trip time of zero seconds, a case protocol designers never expected, and warning of a bug worse than the millennium bug. It is humor, not a real problem report.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8774 is an April 1st joke about protocols that expect messages to take time. It imagines zero round-trip time and shows how some delay-based calculations might fail in that scenario.

subtitle: An April 1st RFC imagines protocol failures when round-trip time reaches zero.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke imagines Internet paths with zero round-trip time, a value that many protocol mechanisms were not designed to handle.
tldr.mechanism: It uses LEDBAT, Multipath TCP, and RTP circuit breakers as examples of calculations or behavior that could fail in the imagined zero-RTT case.
tldr.outcome: The document recommends lower-bounding RTT-based values and using flow control. Its claims about instant quantum Internet paths are the premise of the joke.

today: RFC 8774 is an Informational document published on April 1, 2020. Its zero-delay quantum networking scenario and urgent warnings form a joke, not a report of a deployed network.

sections.title: The Imagined Zero-Delay Path
sections.content: The RFC imagines quantum networking making the measured one-way delay and round-trip time zero. It calls failures caused by this unexpected value “Quantum Bugs.” This scenario and the claim that such networks are imminent are presented in an April 1st document.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke imagines that messages can travel with no measurable delay. It asks what happens to protocols that expect delay to be greater than zero.

sections.title: Examples of Protocol Behavior
sections.content: The RFC examines three examples. It says LEDBAT could keep increasing its congestion window because its queuing-delay measurement would remain zero; MPTCP's alpha calculation includes division by RTT; and a simplified RTP circuit-breaker equation also divides by RTT. These are presented as failures under the imagined zero-RTT condition.
sections.plainLanguage: Some example mechanisms measure delay or divide by it. If the measured delay were zero, the RFC says those calculations could behave incorrectly.

sections.title: The RFC's Proposed Response
sections.content: RFC 8774 proposes lower-bounding values calculated from RTT and using flow control. It says TCP's retransmission timeout is lower-bounded and its receiver window limits transmission. The security section argues that flow control would also be needed to prevent an imagined zero-RTT data flood.
sections.plainLanguage: The document's proposed safeguards are to avoid dividing by RTT and to limit how much data a receiver accepts. These suggestions belong to its humorous scenario.
